The core challenge is constructing a robust mathematical infrastructure capable of handling both fine-grained local phenomena and large-scale global behavior. This requires a hierarchical decomposition where each layer abstracts away irrelevant details while preserving essential structure. In measure theory, this manifests as the monotone class theorem and Dynkin's pi-system lemma, ensuring that properties holding on simple generating sets extend to the full sigma-algebra. For machine learning applications, this translates into scalable inference algorithms (e.g., variational autoencoders) that factorize joint posteriors into tractable conditionals, enabling efficient computation of marginal distributions. The key failure mode is information bottleneck: if the abstraction loses too much detail, downstream decisions become suboptimal; conversely, if it retains excessive complexity, overfitting occurs. Thus, optimal design balances expressiveness against computational feasibility, guided by principles like minimum description length.
